entities.name: Constantine I of Imereti
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Constantine I (Georgian: კონსტანტინე I) reigned as King of Imereti, the western Georgian kingdom, from 1293 until his death in 1327, a period marked by profound political fragmentation and persistent Mongol suzerainty across the broader Georgian realm. As a member of the Bagrationi dynasty, the ancient royal house of Georgia, Constantine inherited a fragment of what was once a powerful, unified kingdom, his rule representing a crucial chapter in Georgia's struggle for independence and the complex geopolitics of the Caucasus during the late medieval period. His reign was largely defined by internal strife with his brother Michael and the ongoing shadow of the Ilkhanate, making him a figure emblematic of fractured sovereignty.

Ascending to the throne following the death of his father, King David VI Narin, Constantine I inherited a kingdom already engaged in a bitter civil war against his brother, Michael. This dynastic struggle, primarily fueled by competing claims to the Imeretian throne and the broader Georgian legacy, consumed much of his early reign, lasting for several years. Despite these internal divisions, Constantine managed to maintain a degree of autonomy for Imereti, distinct from the eastern Georgian kingdoms (Kartli and Kakheti) which remained under more direct Ilkhanid control. His primary achievement was consolidating his rule in Western Georgia, ensuring the continuity of the Imeretian monarchy through turbulent times, though he did not achieve broader Georgian reunification.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Constantine I's reign was significant in preserving the independent Kingdom of Imereti for over three decades, preventing its absorption by the Ilkhanate and maintaining a distinct Georgian royal line in the west. This contributed to the eventual, albeit temporary, reunification of Georgia under George V.
